reference_title: Design and Construction of Driven Pile Foundations

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Static load testing is the most accurate method of determining pile capacity, in design or construction. Reasons: design or construction verification from load-deflection or load-transfer data; confirming the ground's nominal resistance; calibrating resistance factors; p-y response of lateral piles. Prerequisites: subsurface exploration (a load test is no substitute), stratigraphy, static analyses. Jack and load cell 120-150% of the maximum load. AASHTO factors assume one test per site condition: 0.80 with dynamic testing, 0.75 without, 0.60 tension (Table 9-1).
sections.body: 9.1 General (pp. 1-7). Static load testing is the most accurate method of determining load capacity; tests may be in the design or construction stage; types are axial compression, axial tension and lateral. Further detail: current ASTM standards and the NYSDOT Static Pile Load Test Manual GCP-18 (2007). 9.1.1 Reasons: (1) design verification or refinement and construction verification or procedure modification from measured load-deflection or load-transfer data; (2) confirm the ground provides the nominal geotechnical resistance; (3) determine or calibrate resistance factors for new static design methods, local or regional geology, or dynamic or rapid load test methods; (4) determine p-y response of laterally loaded piles. Program development and oversight by an experienced foundation engineer; poorly performed tests can give unsafe or grossly uneconomical foundations. Prerequisites: a detailed subsurface exploration at the test location (a load test is not a substitute), defined stratigraphy with engineering parameters and groundwater, and static analyses to select pile types, lengths and test locations. 9.1.2 Program: goals set first, level of effort differs for confirming resistance versus load-transfer data. Loading apparatus should be able to reach geotechnical failure (one sized only to the anticipated nominal resistance is usually insufficient); jack and load cell capacity 120% to 150% of the anticipated maximum load; load cell, spherical bearing plate, and LVDTs or dial gages with enough travel (shimming and resetting prohibited); toe and intermediate measurements where possible; supervision by an experienced foundation engineer; a full test pile installation record (hammer stroke, fuel/energy setting, cushions, final set, installation aids, times and stops); dynamic monitoring of the test pile recommended. 9.1.3 When and where: at a representative location; number and location by site variability; the AASHTO resistance factor assumes one load test per site condition (Section 5.5.3). Effective uses (after Kyfor et al. 1992): substantial savings; uncertain resistance; zoned variable conditions; higher than typical resistance; setup or relaxation; tension or lateral needs; new design or testing methods; new pile types, large open-end pipe piles or procedures; reuse of existing piles; dynamic and static estimates differing significantly (H-piles that 'run'); local LRFD calibration. 9.1.4 Design-stage tests allow comparing pile types, confirm drivability, set preliminary driving criteria, reduce bid contingency and disputes; construction-stage tests confirm design loads, set production lengths and minimum penetrations. Load test databases (Paikowsky 2004; Abu-Hejleh 2015): an Oregon DOT study (Smith et al. 2011) recommended 0.55 for wave equation at initial driving and 0.40 at restrike; AASHTO (2010) changed phi_dyn for wave equation from 0.40 to 0.50; the FHWA DFLTD holds about 1300 tests (1985-2003). 9.1.5 Resistance factors in Table 9-1; none for lateral load tests, which are governed by service limit deformation criteria.
key_points: Static load test: most accurate method of determining pile capacity; design or construction stage
Reasons include confirming nominal resistance, calibrating resistance factors, and p-y response
A load test is not a substitute for a subsurface exploration program
Jack and load cell capacity 120% to 150% of the anticipated maximum test load
Dynamic monitoring of the static test pile recommended
AASHTO resistance factor assumes one load test per site condition
Table 9-1: phi_dyn 0.80 (static + dynamic testing), 0.75 (static only); phi_up 0.60 (tension)
No resistance factor for lateral load tests: governed by service limit deformation

sections.title: Axial Compression Load Test
sections.summary: ASTM D1143 load is applied by jacking against an anchored beam or a weighted platform; a calibrated load cell is primary, jack pressure secondary, with a spherical bearing plate. AASHTO's quick test: 5% increments of the anticipated nominal resistance, each held 4 to 15 minutes, to nominal resistance or jack capacity. Davisson offset: sf = Delta + (0.15 + b/120) for b <= 24 in.; sf = Delta + b/30 for b > 36 in.; interpolate between. Factored resistance 0.75 to 0.80 of the failure load.
sections.body: 9.2 (pp. 8-19). Piles are most often tested in axial compression: incremental or constant-rate loading at the head, recording time, load and head movement, with optional telltales or strain gages for load transfer (Figure 9-1). 9.2.2 Equipment (ASTM D1143-07, re-approved 2013): jacking against a beam anchored by piles or ground anchors, or a weighted platform; a calibrated load cell is the primary load measure and calibrated jack pressure the secondary; a spherical bearing plate limits eccentricity. Head movement by LVDTs or dial gages on an independent reference beam: ASTM requires 2 in. travel and 0.01 in. precision; 4 in. travel and 0.001 in. are highly recommended; at least two gages diametrically opposite (four often advantageous); a backup scale, mirror and wire (0.01 in.) and a survey level. Reference beam and wire supports, and reaction piles, at least 5 pile diameters and not less than 8 ft clear from the test pile; weighted-platform cribbing more than 5 ft clear. Steel bearing plates between jack, load cell and spherical plate; remote recording recommended. 9.2.3 Loading: AASHTO (2014) recommends the ASTM D1143 quick test (2 to 4 hours): increments of 5% of the anticipated nominal geotechnical resistance (about 20 points), each held no more than 15 and no less than 4 minutes (same interval throughout), readings at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 (and 8, 15) minutes, until nominal resistance or jack capacity within safe structural limits; if plunging, lock off the pump; unload in 5 to 10 equal decrements held 4 to 15 minutes. 9.2.4 Interpretation: methods based on gross movement without elastic deformation are not recommended (overestimate short piles, underestimate long piles). Plot so the elastic line is about 20 degrees from the load axis; Eq 9-1. AASHTO Article 10.7.3.8.2 uses the Davisson (1972) offset limit: the failure load is where the curve meets the offset line (Figure 9-8); no intersection means resistance exceeds the maximum test load. Eq 9-2 for b <= 24 in.; Eq 9-3 for b > 36 in.; interpolate for 24 to 36 in. For H-piles use the flange width as b. Davisson applies to tests with holds of not more than 1 hour; longer holds underestimate resistance. Load cell and jack readings are compared throughout; large discrepancies: unload, resolve, restart. Factored compression resistance is 0.75 (static test only) to 0.80 (with dynamic testing and signal matching) of the failure load. Pile head results alone give no load-transfer detail. 9.2.5 Limitations: cannot account for long-term settlement, downdrag or group action; cost, time, little information on driving stresses or damage; can mislead on highly variable sites. (The print has no heading 9.2.1, though 9.2.4 cites it.)

sections.title: Tension Load Test
sections.summary: Tension tests (ASTM D3689) give uplift resistance, often governing minimum penetration for groups with large uplift (cofferdam seals, segmental construction, seismic, vessel impact, debris). Load is applied by a jack on reaction beams over reaction piles or crane mats, through a center-hole rod or a yoke. The quick test (5% increments, 4-15 min holds) is recommended. AASHTO: modified Davisson, elastic lengthening plus 0.15 in.; factored tension resistance 0.60 of the failure load.
sections.body: 9.3 (pp. 20-23). Tension tests determine axial uplift resistance, often a significant factor in minimum penetration for groups with large uplift demand (cofferdam seals with large buoyancy, cantilever segmental construction, seismic, vessel impact or debris loading); often economical by jacking against a beam on crane mats. 9.3.1 Equipment (ASTM D3689-07, re-approved 2013): a jack centered on reaction beams supported by reaction piles or by mats and cribbing; a center-hole jack with a rod embedded in the pile (common for concrete piles with low tension loads) or a yoke with rods either side of the beam (common for steel piles); load cell primary, jack pressure backup, spherical bearing plate. Gages: ASTM requires 2 in. travel and 0.01 in. precision, 4 in. recommended; at least two diametrically opposite; backup scale, mirror and wire; supports at least 5 diameters and 8 ft clear; survey level backup (Figures 9-9, 9-10). 9.3.2 Loading: the quick test with increments of 5% of the anticipated nominal tension resistance (about 20 points), equal holds of 4 to 15 minutes, readings at 0.5, 1, 2, 4 (8, 15) minutes, to nominal resistance or jack capacity, then unloading in 5 to 10 decrements. Testing to pullout is desirable, especially in design-stage programs; production piles tested in tension during construction should be redriven to the original toe elevation and driving resistance. 9.3.3 Interpretation: no widely accepted method has been published (Fuller 1983 lists gross or net movement limits, curve slope, or offset methods). AASHTO (2014) recommends a modified Davisson method: the failure load is where the curve meets the elastic lengthening plus 0.15 in.; factored tension resistance is 0.60 of it (Figure 9-11).
key_points: ASTM D3689; uplift often governs minimum penetration for groups with large uplift demand

sections.title: Lateral Load Test
sections.summary: Lateral tests (ASTM D3966) have grown with seismic and vessel impact design, noise walls and large signs. Most test a single free-head pile while service piles are fixed-head groups, so the main purpose is to determine or verify p-y curves. Jacking or pulling between two piles is economical; pulling is preferred (two-force member) with at least 20 ft or 20 diameters clear. Deflection versus depth (inclinometer or shape accel array) is strongly recommended. ASTM standard loading reaches 200% of the lateral design load (Table 9-2).
sections.body: 9.4 (pp. 24-31). Lateral tests are run where piles carry significant lateral loads; their importance has grown with extreme event limit states (seismic, vessel impact) and with noise walls and large overhead signs. Most tests are on a single free-head pile, whereas most service piles are fixed-head groups, so results may not apply directly; the primary purpose is to determine the p-y curves for design or verify those used. Jacking or pulling between two piles is often economical, and in design-stage tests the two piles can be different types. 9.4.1 Equipment (ASTM D3966-07, re-approved 2013): a jack against a reaction (piles, deadman, weighted platform) or between two piles; pulling the piles together is preferred, as a two-force member keeps alignment, but ASTM then requires a clear distance of not less than 20 ft or 20 pile diameters. Load cell primary, jack pressure backup; spherical bearing plate(s) unless loading by pulling. Gages on a reference beam perpendicular to movement: ASTM requires 3 in. travel and 0.01 in. precision; backup scale, mirror and wire. Deflection versus depth is strongly recommended, by inclinometer casing read after load holds of 30 minutes or longer, or by a Shape Accel Array (Rollins et al. 2009; triaxial accelerometers in 1 in. PVC casing, 12 in. segments, reusable, static and dynamic); tests measuring only head deflection are seldom justifiable (Kyfor et al. 1992). Otherwise measure head rotation (deflection at two elevations, or a tiltmeter) to assess p-y modelling (Figures 9-12 to 9-16). 9.4.2 Loading: the ASTM D3966 Standard Loading procedure applies 200% of the proposed lateral design load in decreasing increments, holds rising from 10 minutes to 60 minutes at the maximum, then four 50% unloading decrements (Table 9-2); readings before and after each change and at 5 minute intervals, and at 15 and 30 minutes after removal. 9.4.3 Interpretation is more complicated than axial tests: report head load-deflection (Figure 9-17) and deflection versus depth (Figure 9-18) and compare with p-y software predictions (Figure 9-19) to select or validate p-y curves; see Reese (1984) and Kyfor et al. (1992).
key_points: ASTM D3966; growing use for seismic, vessel impact, noise walls and large overhead signs
Single free-head test piles versus fixed-head groups in service: results may not apply directly

sections.title: Load Transfer Evaluations
sections.summary: Shaft and toe resistance come from telltales or strain gages. Two telltales give Qavg = AE(R1 - R2)/L (Eq 9-4); with head and toe readings, toe resistance is Rp = 2Qavg - Q for uniform shaft resistance (Eq 9-5) or Rp = 3Qavg - 2Q for triangular (Eq 9-6). Strain gages give F = eps E A (Eq 9-7), with a composite modulus for concrete-filled pipe (Eq 9-8) and the tangent modulus method for concrete (Eqs 9-9 to 9-12). Residual load from driving alters the computed shaft and toe split, not the total nominal resistance.
sections.body: 9.5 (pp. 32-46). 9.5.1 Telltales: thin steel rods in slightly larger tubes from the head to selected points (Figure 9-20; NYSDOT GCP-18 details); gages on the rods measure relative movement; average load between two points by Eq 9-4 (Kyfor et al. 1992). If R1 and R2 are at head and toe, toe resistance for a uniform resistance distribution (Fellenius 1990) is Eq 9-5, with Q as close to the failure load as possible, or for a linearly increasing (triangular) distribution Eq 9-6; shaft resistance = head load minus toe resistance. 9.5.2 Strain gages: telltales alone are insufficient for detailed load transfer because of residual load; Dunnicliff (1988) suggests weldable vibrating wire gages on steel piles and vibrating wire sister bars in concrete piles; resistance gages serve static and dynamic measurements; an instrumentation specialist should select gages, redundancy and data acquisition. Moisture is a leading cause of resistance gage failure. Gages at pre-selected strata; the uppermost below the head where no shaft resistance acts (Dunnicliff: three undamaged diameters above ground; at least two diameters below the head) for modulus determination, with gage pairs against bending (Figure 9-25); Komurka (2015) adds a level two diameters above the toe; toe sister bars hung from the head in concrete-filled pipe. Force by Eq 9-7; composite modulus by Eq 9-8; concrete modulus falls with strain, so Fellenius (2001) recommends the tangent modulus method: plot tangent modulus versus strain, fit slope A and intercept B (Figure 9-26), Eqs 9-9 to 9-12. Example (Figure 9-27): 14 in. concrete-filled pipe, 53.9 - 37.6 = 16.3 tons over 12.3 ft x 3.67 ft = 45.1 ft2 gives 0.36 tsf, ignoring residual load. 9.5.3 Residual load: locked in when the pile does not fully rebound, especially flexible piles, large shaft resistance or large toe quake; it gives negative shaft resistance in the upper pile, can double the apparent shaft resistance and underestimates toe resistance (Figures 9-28 to 9-30, Fellenius 2014); the nominal resistance is unaffected but the shaft and toe split changes, which matters for uplift from compression tests. Take zero readings before installation; the strain change between just before the test and true no-load is a lower bound (Fellenius et al. 2003). Fellenius (2002b) method (Figure 9-31): true resistance follows half the measured shaft resistance to the inflection, then is extrapolated; judgment is needed.
key_points: Telltales: Eq 9-4 Qavg = AE(R1 - R2)/L (Kyfor et al. 1992)
Eq 9-5: Rp = 2Qavg - Q (uniform); Eq 9-6: Rp = 3Qavg - 2Q (triangular)
Telltales alone are insufficient for detailed load transfer because of residual load
Weldable vibrating wire gages on steel piles; vibrating wire sister bars in concrete piles (Dunnicliff 1988)
Top gage level at least two diameters below the head, where no shaft resistance acts
Eq 9-7: F = eps E A; Eq 9-8: composite modulus of concrete-filled steel piles
Tangent modulus method (Fellenius 2001), Eqs 9-9 to 9-12: Esm = 0.5 A eps + B

sections.title: Practical Issues and Considerations
sections.summary: Static load tests are the most reliable and most expensive method; cost alone should not decide. Delays come from adding tests late: decide early in design; in construction, specify the number and locations of tests and the engineer's review time, and require the test before pile lengths are ordered or production driving starts. Load cell and jack readings that disagree must be resolved (jack exceeded load cell by 10-20% in one case). Size load cells and jacks to match.
sections.body: 9.6 (pp. 46-48). Static load tests are the most reliable and most expensive method for nominal geotechnical resistance or lateral deformation; while their economics should be considered, cost alone should not decide; load transfer and deflected-shape data are extremely valuable when evaluated by knowledgeable instrumentation specialists, who should be involved in program development. Delays usually occur when tests are added late: in design, decide early whether to test; in construction, clearly specify the number and locations of tests and the engineer's review time, and state that the test must be performed before ordering pile lengths or starting production driving, so the contractor can schedule. Fellenius (1984): after a questionable first test, a rerun with a new load cell and recalibrated system still showed the jack pressure load exceeding the load cell by 10 to 20% in loading and under it by 5% in unloading (Figure 9-32); discrepancies must be found and the test rerun if needed. Load cells and jacks should be properly sized: Geokon (2013) found load cell error when the cell and jack piston diameters differ, compounded by thin bearing plates (Figure 9-33: one 4 in. I.D., 5-3/4 in. O.D., 300 kip load cell with three jack sizes).
key_points: Most reliable and most expensive method; cost alone should not be the deciding factor
Decide early in design whether to test; late additions cause delays
Construction stage: specify number and locations of tests and engineer review time
Test before ordering pile lengths or starting production driving
Load cell and jack pressure disagreements must be resolved; rerun if needed
Match load cell and jack piston diameters; use sufficiently thick bearing plates

sections.title: Advantages, Disadvantages, and Limitations
sections.summary: Advantages: a more rational design, considerably more reliable than static analyses or dynamic formulas; possible shorter piles or higher factored loads; resistance factors of 0.75 to 0.80 versus 0.40 for the Modified Gates formula; confirmation at the planned penetration. Disadvantages: cost, setup and interpretation time, little information on driving stresses or damage; misleading on highly variable sites. Limitations: no account of long-term settlement, downdrag or group action.
sections.body: 9.7 (pp. 48-49). Advantages: (1) a more rational design, as confirmation of resistance by static load testing is considerably more reliable than static analyses and dynamic formulas; (2) improved knowledge of pile-soil behavior may allow shorter piles or higher factored loads; (3) a higher resistance factor, 0.75 to 0.80 when static load tests are used compared with 0.40 for the Modified Gates dynamic formula; (4) confirmation that the factored load is supported at the planned penetration. Disadvantages: test cost, time to set up and perform, time for complete interpretation (especially load transfer data), and minimal information on driving stresses or pile damage; results can mislead on highly variable sites, so site size and variability should be considered when relying on a single test pile. Limitations: results cannot account for long-term settlement, downdrag from consolidating and settling soils, or group action.
